asDecan.p: A sign has three decans of ten degrees, each with a ruling planet and a small card. Your Sun falls in the first ten degrees of Virgo, where the sign is newest and most itself, and in the Chaldean order those degrees belong to the Sun. So your Sun sits in its own slice, though that wins it no dignity. It's a visitor in Virgo, neither helped nor held back, and it takes its manner from Mercury, who rules the sign, so its pride goes into getting things right. On the card a man sits bent over a bench with a chisel, finished coins hung up beside him and the town a long way off. The Nine of Pentacles, Venus's slice, is about enjoying what the work paid for, and the Ten, Mercury's, about what gets handed down. Yours is the slice still at the bench. It's the hands-on end of The Hermit, who is Virgo's Major and so your Sun card, and most early Virgo Suns I've met wouldn't want to be anywhere else.

You're the person who reads the manual. Someone unboxes a new coffee machine and everyone else starts pressing buttons, and you're on page four finding out what the descaling light means. On a free Saturday you pick up a small job, regrouting the shower or relearning a guitar part you've played slightly wrong for years, and three hours go by. At a family dinner someone says the pie's lovely and you tell them the pastry shrank at one end. With the Sun here, doing a thing well is how you feel like yourself, and being bad at something new makes you quietly cross. I see this a lot with early Virgo Suns. There's plenty of pride in you. It goes into the finish on the work, and you'd go a bit red if anyone called it that.

You can make other people good at things without making them feel stupid. You learned slowly yourself, one repetition at a time, so you still remember which bit was confusing. When a new starter is lost in the booking system, you're the one who sits with them for twenty minutes and shows them the three steps that matter and the ten they can ignore. You taught your nephew to drive and nobody shouted. Friends ring you before they tackle the flat-pack wardrobe or their first tax return, and the time after that they don't need to. The Sun brings enough warmth that your teaching doesn't land as a correction, and Mercury gives you the patience to break a job into pieces. Years later people thank you for something you've completely forgotten showing them.

You find it hard to like yourself on a day you haven't made or fixed anything. Leave you on the couch for an afternoon and you get faintly miserable, then go looking for a job to make the feeling stop. On holiday you last about two days before you're reorganising the rental's kitchen drawers. A quiet superiority creeps in too. You watch a colleague rush a job and privately file them as someone who doesn't care, when they're juggling a sick kid and two deadlines. The Sun wants to be seen, and in Virgo it wants to be seen being careful, so you do extra polish nobody asked for, partly hoping someone notices, and resent it when they don't. None of that gets said. It comes out sideways, as a tight little remark about how the towels were folded, and whoever folded them has no idea where it came from.

Something goes badly, a friendship ends, a death in the family, the job you trained for goes to someone else, and you go and make something. You're in the shed or at the desk until late, rebuilding the side gate or redoing a spreadsheet that was fine. For a few days it genuinely settles you. A week on you're running on empty, because the Sun is your vitality and you've been pouring all of it into the work. Your back aches, you've eaten standing up for days, and you're pulling apart things you finished last week. The people at home mostly see the back of your head. There's no job they can do to your standard, so they stop offering. What does help is putting the tools down at a set hour, letting someone sit with you while you work, and telling them what happened before you've found the right words.

You love by getting good at someone. You learn which part of the week is hard for them, how warm they like the bedroom, the exact thing to say after a bad phone call with their mum, and you keep refining it for years. Being learned back is much harder. It feels exposing to be studied that closely, and when a partner gets something right about you, you tend to brush it off or change the subject. Early on you can seem reserved, because you'd like to be sure you're good at this before you show much of it, which is a bit like wanting to swim well before getting in the pool. A partner who's loose with plans or vague with promises wears on you, and you'll say so, sometimes too precisely. The ones who last are steady, notice the effort, and tell you they noticed.

The Hermit gives you the wish to understand a thing all the way down, and this slice adds the hands. You do best with a real craft and a standard to meet, joinery, dentistry, editing, code, anywhere a practised hand is plainly better than a new one. You're a strong apprentice and later a strong trainer, and managers learn fast that what you hand in doesn't need checking. You're slow to call a job finished, so deadlines slide while you fix things nobody else would see. The bigger cost is getting so absorbed in the work that you skip the people side of the job. You miss the Friday drinks and the corridor chat where decisions get made, and then someone less skilled who was in the room gets the role you wanted. Go to the next one of those and spend five minutes telling someone what you're working on.

In your twenties this slice is usually intense about getting good. You pick something and practise it hard, and you can be so harsh with yourself when progress is slow that you drop a thing you loved because it didn't come fast enough. Plenty of people with this placement have one of those somewhere, a violin in a cupboard or a quilt with four squares done. By the mid-thirties most have real mastery in at least one area, and the question shifts to whether the work still means anything. A lot change direction around then, often into teaching, or into a small business where they set the standard. The fifties tend to loosen the grip. Most can leave a job at ninety per cent and sleep fine, and they start enjoying what they're good at and get generous with it, fixing the neighbour's fence, giving away the jam, taking on an apprentice.

For a month, whenever someone praises a thing you've made or done, the dinner, the report, the shelves in the hall, say thank you and leave it there. Don't point out the corner that isn't square or the bit of sauce that split. If the flaw comes out anyway, and at first it probably will, put a pencil tick on the kitchen calendar and carry on. Nobody else needs to know what the ticks are for. For most people with this decan they thin out by about the third week.
